docs.title: Hype vs. evidence
docs.text:
“Lion’s Mane regrows your brain.”

Rated D overall; at most C− for mild cognitive impairment.

“Dihexa is millions of times stronger than BDNF.”

No checkable publication supports this claim.

“Bacopa works right away.”

Rated B for memory, but only after at least 12 weeks.

“Creatine is just for the gym.”

Rated B for vegetarians, older adults and sleep-deprived people.

“Caffeine is too basic.”

One of only three A ratings in the course: vigilance and attention, especially under fatigue.

docs.title: Module 0 – Introduction and Evidence Framework
docs.text:
Educational content only

This course describes research evidence. It is not medical advice, and study doses are reported only so the evidence can be judged. Several substances are prescription-only, controlled or have never been evaluated for human safety.

docs.title: 0.1 Purpose, Scope and Disclaimer
docs.text:
Few areas of pharmacology have as wide a gap between public enthusiasm and controlled evidence as cognitive enhancement. At one end sit compounds with decades of mechanistic work and dozens of RCTs, such as caffeine, whose adenosine pharmacology is among the best-characterized receptor systems in the CNS. At the other end sit peptides and synthetic analogs whose entire human evidence base fits in a single, developer-authored paper from the 1970s. Online sources and vendors routinely present both ends in the same register of confident promise. This course aims to restore the gradient between them.

The course is written for readers comfortable with receptor pharmacology, signal transduction, and the basic vocabulary of clinical trial design. It treats each substance the way a critical review article would: what is known about its chemistry and disposition, what it does at the molecular level, what happens when it is actually tested in humans, and how much confidence those tests deserve.

This is an educational text, not medical advice. The dose ranges reported in each monograph describe what was administered in the studies discussed, so readers can judge the evidence. They are not recommendations, and they say nothing about safety for any individual. Several substances covered here are prescription-only or controlled, and several have never undergone formal human safety evaluation at all.

docs.title: 0.2 The A–E Evidence Rating System
docs.text:
Every monograph ends with a letter rating. To keep these ratings reproducible rather than impressionistic, they follow a fixed set of criteria, loosely modeled on the GRADE framework used in clinical guideline development.

Rating Criteria Typical profile A Multiple independent, adequately powered RCTs or meta-analyses; consistent direction and magnitude of effect; low risk of bias Replicated across labs and funding sources; effect survives meta-analytic correction for publication bias B Several RCTs, but with heterogeneity, modest sample sizes, or limited independent replication Effect is probably real, but its size or boundary conditions are uncertain C Few or inconsistent human trials, or effects demonstrated only in clinical or deficient populations Plausible benefit in specific contexts; transfer to healthy users unestablished D Isolated human studies with high risk of bias, or predominantly animal data with some human signal Hypothesis-generating at best E Preclinical (in vitro, rodent) or anecdotal data only No basis for inferring human efficacy

Starting from the level of the available study designs, a rating is lowered when one of five problems is present. Risk of bias covers inadequate randomization, unblinding (a serious issue for psychoactive substances with noticeable subjective effects), selective outcome reporting, and manufacturer involvement in design or analysis. Inconsistency means trials disagree in direction or magnitude of effect without a convincing explanation. Indirectness means the studied population, outcome, or formulation differs from what users actually take. Imprecision means small samples and wide confidence intervals that cross zero or trivial effect sizes. Finally, a rating drops when there is evidence or strong suspicion of publication bias.

Ratings are population-specific. Many compounds show clear effects under deficit conditions and little or nothing in rested, well-nourished, healthy adults. Creatine's cognitive effects concentrate in vegetarians, older adults, and sleep-deprived subjects. Tyrosine's effects show up under acute stressors that deplete catecholamines. Ratings are therefore given per population where the data diverge, for example "B (sleep-deprived) / C (rested healthy adults)."

Ratings describe efficacy, not safety. A compound can have weak efficacy evidence and a well-characterized safety profile, or modest efficacy evidence and an essentially unknown long-term risk profile. Each monograph therefore adds a safety-knowledge descriptor:

Descriptor Meaning Well characterized Long human use history, pharmacovigilance data, known interaction profile Partially characterized Short- to medium-term trial safety data; long-term and rare adverse events largely unknown Uncharacterized No systematic human safety data; risks must be treated as unknown, not absent

Effect sizes are reported as standardized mean differences (Cohen's d or Hedges' g) where available. The conventional benchmarks of 0.2 (small), 0.5 (medium) and 0.8 (large) are used with a caveat: in healthy young adults, even well-established pharmacological enhancers usually produce effects at the small end of that range on objective cognitive tests. A finding of d ≈ 0.2–0.3 in this population is roughly what the ceiling of the field looks like. Claims of large effects in healthy people should be read as a warning sign about study quality rather than as evidence of an exceptional compound.

Effect sizes computed from Cohen's d, assuming normal distributions with equal spread.

At d = 0.25, roughly the ceiling for well-established enhancers in healthy young adults, most treated people score no differently from most untreated people. The overlap and above-average shares are calculated directly from d, assuming normal distributions with equal spread.

Each substance placed by its best rating in any population, from Appendix A.

The three A ratings all come from relieving a deficit; for enhancement in rested, healthy adults, the best-supported substances sit at B or lower. Where Appendix A gives a split rating such as B−/C, the substance is placed in the lower tier.

docs.title: 0.3 Epistemic Conventions
docs.text:
Throughout the course, statements are marked by their evidential status whenever the distinction matters.

  • [Established] marks findings supported by replicated human data or by well-characterized pharmacology that is not seriously disputed.
  • [Hypothesis] marks mechanistically plausible accounts with some supporting evidence that have not been directly confirmed in humans.
  • [Speculation] marks extrapolations beyond the data, included only when they help frame open questions.

Citation policy. Specific studies are named only when author, year and journal are known with confidence. Where the literature is described in general terms, or a detail could not be pinned down with certainty, the text carries the marker [verify source]. No reference in this course is invented. Readers who want to build on a claim should check the primary literature, especially for older Soviet- and Russian-language work, which is often hard to access and was rarely independently replicated.

docs.title: 0.4 How to Read the Monographs
docs.text:
Each substance chapter follows the same nine-part structure: Origin & History, Chemistry, Pharmacokinetics, Pharmacodynamics, Evidence Base, Doses Used in Studies, Safety, Legal Status, and Evidence Rating. The order is deliberate. Pharmacokinetics comes before pharmacodynamics because a compelling mechanism is irrelevant if the molecule doesn't reach its target. The evidence section comes before the dose section, so that doses are read as properties of specific studies rather than as free-floating numbers.

Module placement reflects a preliminary estimate. The rating at the end of each monograph is the result of the analysis and sometimes differs.

docs.title: Module 1 – Foundations
docs.text:
Educational content only

This course describes research evidence. It is not medical advice, and study doses are reported only so the evidence can be judged. Several substances are prescription-only, controlled or have never been evaluated for human safety.

docs.title: 1.1 Definition and History of the Nootropic Concept
docs.text:
The term nootropic was coined by the Romanian-born neurophysiologist Corneliu Giurgea in a French-language paper in 1972 (Actualités Pharmacologiques 25:115–156), while working at the Belgian company UCB, where piracetam had been synthesized in 1964 and was marketed from 1971. The concept was built around piracetam's pharmacology, so its originator was also employed by the company selling the first nootropic. In animal models piracetam protected learned behavior against hypoxia and electroconvulsive shock without clear sedative or GABAergic effects, and Giurgea proposed it as a new pharmacological class.

According to Giurgea, a nootropic should:

  1. Enhance learning and memory.
  2. Increase the resistance of learned behavior to disruptive conditions (hypoxia, electroconvulsive shock, scopolamine).
  3. Protect the brain against physical or chemical injury.
  4. Increase the efficacy of tonic cortical and subcortical control mechanisms.
  5. Lack the usual pharmacology of psychotropic drugs (no sedation, no motor stimulation), with very few side effects and extremely low toxicity.

These criteria were derived almost entirely from rodent paradigms, whose translation to human cognition has proven poor. The fifth criterion also excludes most substances that actually produce measurable effects in humans. [Established] Strictly applied, almost no substance with replicated human efficacy meets all five criteria, and the substances that come closest to criterion five (racetams) have the weakest human efficacy data.

Category Defining feature Examples Psychostimulant enhancers Catecholaminergic or adenosinergic arousal Caffeine, methylphenidate, modafinil Cholinergic agents Precursors, esterase inhibitors, receptor modulators Citicoline, Alpha-GPC, donepezil Glutamatergic modulators AMPA/NMDA modulation Aniracetam (hypothesized), memantine Metabolic/structural agents Energy buffering, membrane composition Creatine, omega-3 fatty acids Neurotrophic candidates Claimed induction of BDNF/NGF or growth-factor signaling Lion's Mane, Semax, Dihexa Adaptogens/phytochemicals Multi-target botanical extracts; stress-axis modulation Rhodiola, Bacopa, ginseng

docs.title: 1.2 Neurotransmitter Systems Relevant to Cognition
docs.text:
Cholinergic system. Cortical and hippocampal acetylcholine derives mainly from the basal forebrain (nucleus basalis of Meynert, medial septum, diagonal band). [Established] Cholinergic tone is closely linked to attention, encoding, and cue detection. The homomeric α7 nAChR has high Ca²⁺ permeability and modulates glutamate release and plasticity; α4β2 is the high-affinity nicotine site involved in attention. M1 (Gq, cortex and hippocampus) is the muscarinic subtype most tied to memory, shown most clearly by the pro-amnestic effect of scopolamine, the standard challenge model in nootropic research. Under high demand, choline uptake via CHT1 (SLC5A7) is rate-limiting for acetylcholine synthesis. [Hypothesis] Choline donor supplementation assumes choline supply limits synthesis, which is doubtful in well-nourished humans.

Glutamatergic system. AMPA receptors (GluA1–4) mediate most fast excitatory current; their kinetics are defined by deactivation and desensitization, which positive allosteric modulators slow. [Hypothesis] for the racetams, since relevant in vitro concentrations often exceed plausible brain levels. NMDA receptors are coincidence detectors requiring glutamate, a co-agonist, and depolarization to relieve the Mg²⁺ block. GluN2A-containing receptors dominate synaptically in the adult forebrain; GluN2B-containing receptors are enriched extrasynaptically and linked to both plasticity and excitotoxic signaling. Too little NMDA activity impairs plasticity; too much is excitotoxic.

Catecholaminergic systems. Dopaminergic VTA projections and noradrenergic locus coeruleus projections are central to working memory and executive control. [Established] Prefrontal function follows an inverted-U dose-response curve: both too little and too much D1 stimulation impair working-memory-related persistent firing. Moderate noradrenaline acts on α2A receptors, which reduce cAMP and close HCN channels on dendritic spines, strengthening network connectivity (Wang et al., 2007, Cell). High noradrenaline during stress recruits α1 and β receptors and weakens PFC function. Mattay et al. (2003, PNAS) showed that amphetamine improved prefrontal efficiency during a working-memory task in COMT val/val carriers (presumably lower prefrontal dopamine), whereas in met/met carriers it had no effect at low-to-moderate load and worsened efficiency at the highest load. The effect of a dose depends on where the individual starts on the curve.

Adenosinergic system. Adenosine accumulates with neuronal activity and energy turnover and acts as a homeostatic brake on arousal. A1 receptors (Gi/o) inhibit presynaptic release; A2A receptors (Gs/olf) are concentrated in the striatum and form heteromers with D2 receptors. [Established] Caffeine's arousal effects are mediated primarily by antagonism at these receptors.

GABAergic, serotonergic and histaminergic modulation. GABAergic inhibition shapes gamma and theta oscillations; GABA-A positive modulators such as benzodiazepines are reliably amnestic. 5-HT4 agonism increases hippocampal acetylcholine release. [Established] The failure of 5-HT6 antagonists (idalopirdine, intepirdine) in phase III Alzheimer's trials shows robust rodent procognitive effects failing to translate. H3 inverse agonism (pitolisant) promotes wakefulness and helps explain modafinil's downstream effects.

System Main cognitive domains Key receptors/transporters Typical pharmacological handles Cholinergic Attention, encoding, cue detection α7, α4β2, M1, CHT1, AChE Precursors, AChE inhibitors, nicotinic agonists Glutamatergic Plasticity, learning, consolidation AMPA, NMDA (GluN2A/2B), mGluR AMPA PAMs, NMDA antagonists Dopaminergic Working memory, motivation, flexibility D1 (PFC), D2 (striatum), DAT, COMT DAT inhibitors, precursors Noradrenergic Arousal, working memory, attention α2A, α1, β, NET NET inhibitors, α2A agonists Adenosinergic Arousal, vigilance A1, A2A Antagonists (caffeine) GABAergic Oscillatory timing, anxiety GABA-A subtypes, GABA-B PAMs (amnestic) Serotonergic Mood, flexibility, memory 5-HT1A, 5-HT4, 5-HT6 Subtype-selective ligands Histaminergic Wakefulness H1, H3 H3 inverse agonists

docs.title: 1.3 Neuroplasticity and Neurotrophins
docs.text:
Synaptic plasticity. LTP was first described by Bliss and Lømo (1973, Journal of Physiology). In E-LTP, NMDA-mediated Ca²⁺ influx activates CaMKII, which autophosphorylates at Thr286, phosphorylates GluA1 at Ser831, and promotes AMPA receptor insertion; PKA contributes via GluA1 Ser845. L-LTP requires CREB phosphorylation at Ser133, gene transcription (including BDNF), and spine remodeling. LTD involves calcineurin, PP1, and AMPA internalization. [Hypothesis] Plasticity is a regulated signal-to-noise process, and indiscriminate facilitation could strengthen irrelevant associations as readily as relevant ones.

BDNF. Mature BDNF binds TrkB and activates PI3K/Akt, MAPK/ERK, and PLCγ cascades, required for hippocampal L-LTP. proBDNF binds p75NTR with sortilin and promotes LTD and spine retraction. Egan et al. (2003, Cell) showed that the Val66Met Met allele impairs activity-dependent BDNF secretion and is associated with poorer episodic memory. Later replication has not held up: a meta-analysis of 23 publications with 7,095 people found no significant association between Val66Met and any cognitive phenotype (Mandelman & Grigorenko, 2012, Genes, Brain and Behavior 11:127–136, doi:10.1111/j.1601-183X.2011.00738.x).

Methodological caution. Serum BDNF is dominated by platelet stores released during clotting and is affected by exercise, time of day, and handling. [Established] A rise in serum BDNF is not evidence of increased central neurotrophic signaling, let alone of cognitive benefit.

NGF. NGF acts via TrkA and p75NTR and is essential for basal forebrain cholinergic neurons. [Established] It does not cross the BBB, and intracerebroventricular NGF in early Alzheimer's trials caused pain and weight loss. Raising NGF is neither easy to achieve in the right place nor clearly beneficial when achieved non-selectively.

docs.title: 1.4 Cerebral Energy Metabolism
docs.text:
[Established] The brain accounts for about 2% of body mass but about 20% of resting energy consumption, mostly spent on Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Glucose enters via GLUT1 and GLUT3. The astrocyte–neuron lactate shuttle (Pellerin & Magistretti, 1994, PNAS) proposes that astrocytic glycolysis supplies lactate to neurons via MCTs; [Hypothesis] its quantitative importance in vivo remains debated.

The phosphocreatine/creatine kinase system buffers ATP at sites of high turnover. The brain synthesizes creatine and also takes it up via SLC6A8 at the blood–brain barrier, but only in limited amounts, which limits the brain increase from supplementation (Braissant, 2012, Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease 35:655–664, doi:10.1007/s10545-011-9433-2); Dechent et al. (1999) measured a rise of roughly 8–9% (Module 2.3). SLC6A8 loss-of-function causes a severe creatine deficiency syndrome, showing that brain creatine is essential, not that extra creatine helps. [Established] Restoring mitochondrial function in deficit models is different from enhancing normal function in healthy tissue. Ketone bodies matter mainly in fasting and in conditions with impaired glucose use.

docs.title: 1.5 The Blood–Brain Barrier
docs.text:
The BBB is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells with tight junctions (claudin-5, occludin, ZO proteins), supported by pericytes and astrocytic end-feet.

Property Typical CNS-favorable range Molecular weight < ~450 Da TPSA < ~90 Å² Hydrogen-bond donors ≤ 3 logP Moderate, roughly 2–4 Ionization Minimal charge at physiological pH Transporter Substrates Relevance LAT1 (SLC7A5) Tyrosine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, leucine Tyrosine competes with other LNAAs CTL1, OCTs Choline Limited, saturable uptake MFSD2A DHA as LPC-DHA Main DHA route (Nguyen et al., 2014, Nature) SLC6A8 Creatine Limits brain creatine increase MCT1 Lactate, ketone bodies Energy substrates GLUT1 Glucose Primary energy supply

Efflux transporters (P-gp/ABCB1, BCRP/ABCG2) pump many lipophilic compounds back into blood; P-gp substrate status has never been tested for most nootropics. [Established] Peptides generally have minimal BBB penetration and poor oral bioavailability. [Hypothesis] Nose-to-brain delivery exists, but the fraction reaching the brain is usually very small and, for most peptide nootropics, never quantified in humans. The question "Does it reach the target?" should come before "What does it do at the target?"

docs.title: 1.6 Methodology of Cognition Research
docs.text:
Domain Typical tests Sustained attention/vigilance PVT, CPT, SART Working memory n-back, digit span, spatial working memory Episodic memory RAVLT, word-list recall, paired-associate learning Executive function Stroop, Trail Making B, Wisconsin Card Sorting, stop-signal Processing speed Digit Symbol Substitution, reaction time Subjective state Visual analogue scales, POMS

Standardized batteries include CANTAB, the CDR System, and Cogstate; they generate many outcomes per session, which creates a multiple-testing problem.

Typical weaknesses include practice effects, ceiling effects in healthy young people, uncorrected multiple testing, and low power. Button et al. (2013, Nature Reviews Neuroscience) estimated the median power of neuroscience studies at about 21%, which also inflates significant effect sizes. Improvements may reflect restoration rather than enhancement, as with caffeine withdrawal reversal (James & Rogers, 2005, Psychopharmacology 182:1–8, doi:10.1007/s00213-005-0084-6; Rogers et al., 2013, Module 2.1). Baseline dependency can hide opposing subgroup effects. Substances with noticeable effects are hard to blind, and few trials assess blinding. Most trials are short and rely on surrogate endpoints. Manufacturer funding, publication bias, and hard-to-access, unreplicated Soviet/Russian literature further distort the picture.

Question Warning sign Pre-registered with a primary endpoint? Positive result on a secondary or unspecified measure Sample large enough? n < 50 with a claimed medium-to-large effect Who was studied? Deficient or clinical population generalized to healthy users Blinding assessed? Noticeable subjective effects, blinding untested Multiple comparisons corrected? One significant subtest among many Who funded it? Manufacturer, without independent replication Independent replication? All positive data from one lab or one country Plausible given PK? Mechanism based on concentrations never shown in brain

docs.title: 2.1 Caffeine
docs.text:
Origin & History. Caffeine is the most widely consumed psychoactive substance in the world. Friedlieb Ferdinand Runge first isolated it from coffee in 1819, by common account at Goethe's suggestion; Emil Fischer achieved the first total synthesis.

Evidence rating. A for vigilance, attention and reaction time, especially under fatigue. B/C for memory and higher-order cognition in rested, non-tolerant people. Safety knowledge: well characterized.

Origin & History. A non-proteinogenic amino acid found almost only in tea, identified in 1949 by Yajiro Sakato (Nippon Nogei Kagaku Kaishi 23:262–267). The dominant branded form (Suntheanine, Taiyo Kagaku) funded much early human research.

Evidence rating. C alone. B− for the acute combination on attention switching and alertness. Safety knowledge: partially characterized.

docs.title: Module 3 – Moderately Supported Substances

This course describes research evidence. It is not medical advice, and study doses are reported only so the evidence can be judged. Several substances are prescription-only, controlled or have never been evaluated for human safety.

Evidence rating. C for fatigue under stress; D for rested healthy people. Safety: partially characterized.

Most of the risk from nootropic use comes not from any single substance at typical doses but from combinations, repeated use, and their interaction with a person's medications and physiology.
